## Description

Padé approximant is a rational function approximation expanded from a function value and the derivative function values similar to Taylor Series. Often, Padé approximant's can converge when Taylor Series does not even though both use the same information at a point. The key is Taylor Series is a polynomial while Padé approximant is a rational function. Rational functions can have singularities/vertical-asymptotes and horizontal asymptotes. Polynomials do not have asymptotes or singularities.

Padé approximation replaces a polynomial truncation with a ratio of two polynomials,

$$
R_{m,n}(x)=\frac{P_m(x)}{Q_n(x)},\qquad Q_n(x_0)=1,
$$

and chooses coefficients so the Taylor expansion of $R_{m,n}$ about $x_0$ matches the target function through order $m+n$. Equivalently, $f^{(k)}(x_0)=R_{m,n}^{(k)}(x_0)$ for $k=0,\dots,m+n$. When Taylor coefficients vanish, as for even or odd functions or when $f(x_0)=0$, some entries $[m/n]$ have no such $R_{m,n}$. Those frames show the lower-order entry that takes their place in the Padé table, which matches $f$ only to a lower order, and the legend says so, for example "Padé [2/1] = [1/0] (degenerate)".

Compared with a Taylor polynomial of the same total order, Padé approximants can represent poles and often stay accurate on larger intervals, especially for functions with nearby singularities or branch-point behavior.

High-order Padé Approximants can be hard to compute because the linear system for the denominator coefficients can become badly conditioned as the order rises (for $\sqrt{x}$ about $x_0=5$, the $[4/6]$ system has condition number about $1.5\times10^{11}$), and because that system is singular for some entries $[m/n]$, the degenerate entries described above. MATLAB's symbolic `pade` can be very slow for some entries below total order (numerator plus denominator order) 20: with the 20-digit `vpa` setting of the video script, the $[1/15]$, $[1/16]$ and $[1/17]$ entries for $e^x$ about 0 took about 7, 31 and 134 seconds in MATLAB R2026a. `padeapprox` from chebfun also struggles. It takes a lot of effort to compute a high-order Padé approximate.

The most useful way to understand Padé approximant is to watch the animations below. For details on the construction, see the resources section below.

## Outside Links

[Wikipedia Padé approximate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pad%C3%A9_approximant) - A good overview of Pade's approximate.

[Matlab Symbolic Pade Approximant Page](https://www.mathworks.com/help/releases/R2025b/symbolic/sym.pade.html)

[Chebfun](http://www.chebfun.org/) has a function called `padeapprox` that calculates a Padé approximant numerically. `padeapprox` is based on this paper, [Robust Padé Approximation via SVD](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/110853236).

## Animations

Each animation shows one Padé order per frame for a fixed center $x_0$, overlaid on the target function. Unlike Mathews' surviving original animations, which stepped along the diagonal (or next-to-diagonal) entries of the Padé table, up to total order 18, and marked a tolerance interval, these step through every entry $[m/n]$ with $m+n\le 10$ ($m+n\le 8$ in Cases 12, 17 and 22–27).

[Julia source for all cases](pade_animations_all.jl)
